analysis.one_liner: Requires officials to put their stock holdings in blind trusts or report every trade within three business days.
analysis.headline: A bill to force members of Congress to disclose stock trades or use blind trusts never left committee and got no vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the President, Vice President, members of Congress, and certain federal officials to either place all their stocks, bonds, and commodities futures in a qualified blind trust, or file a report with an ethics office within three business days after any trade settles. Violators would face civil penalties up to $50,000 and possible criminal fines. It was introduced in December 2011 during a wave of congressional stock-trading bills and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans who want to know whether the people writing laws are profiting from those laws. Members' spouses and dependent children's jointly held accounts would be covered too, closing a common workaround.

how_it_helps.text: Requires covered officials to choose between a qualified blind trust — where investments are managed without their knowledge — and near-real-time disclosure of every trade within three business days of settlement [S2][S3].
Covers stocks, bonds, commodities futures, and other securities, including holdings shared with a spouse or dependent child [S2][S3].
Imposes civil penalties up to $50,000 and criminal fines for knowingly and willfully falsifying reports or failing to file them [S3].
Exempts ordinary federal retirement accounts, the Thrift Savings Plan, and Social Security benefits, so no one is forced to divest retirement savings [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress, the President, and other covered officials lose the ability to quietly trade securities based on nonpublic knowledge of legislation and policy, and bear compliance and penalty costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Lawmakers and officials who trade stocks

drawbacks.text: The disclosure option leaves an opening critics of similar bills have noted: a trade reported three business days after settlement can still occur before the public learns of it, so officials could still trade on inside knowledge of pending legislation [S3].
Enforcement depends on the Attorney General choosing to sue a covered official, which means penalties may rarely be applied in practice [S3].
The bill does not ban trading outright; an official willing to accept public scrutiny could keep trading securities that their own committee work might move [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit — knowing quickly when lawmakers buy and sell securities, or removing the temptation entirely through blind trusts — is real and the direct cost is limited to officials' convenience. The three-business-day disclosure window and reliance on Justice Department enforcement are real weaknesses: the bill is a meaningful transparency step but not a full prohibition on trading on nonpublic information.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to three committees, one of which passed it to a subcommittee, and none of them ever acted on it before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Sean Duffy introduced the bill on December 2, 2011 [S1][S5].

The Speaker referred it to three committees at once — Oversight and Government Reform, House Administration, and Judiciary — a multi-committee referral that requires more chairs to act before a bill can move [S5].
Three days later, the Judiciary Committee referred it to its Subcommittee on the Constitution, where it sat [S5].
No hearing, markup, floor vote, or further action of any kind appears in the record for the rest of the 112th Congress [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Members of Congress and other covered officials keep the ability to trade stocks, bonds, and commodities futures without near-real-time disclosure. The broader disclosure debate was later addressed by a different bill in this Congress, but this bill itself died with no vote.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was small and bipartisan (5 Republicans, 1 Democrat), and no vote was ever recorded, so the partisan shape of opposition cannot be measured from the record.

industries.industry: Members of Congress and senior federal officials (officeholders as a class)
industries.note: The bill would force them to either give up personal control of their securities portfolios or disclose every trade within three business days, including jointly held spousal accounts. Inaction in committee preserved the status quo, where annual disclosure is far less timely.

Trading by officials is a small slice of brokerage business, and a three-day disclosure rule could shift some officials into blind trusts, whose trustees still trade through brokers. The direct effect on the industry is modest.
